claim: A trained working method is kept after a better one exists: after five long-method problems about 80% of people use the long method on critical problems that have a shorter one; controls without training almost never do (0.83 vs 0.00 in Binz and Schulz, N=310).
agent_test: Give the agent a first working method in-context (3-5 solved examples), then critical items with a shorter route; measure shortcut rate vs a no-example control at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The effect grows with the amount of training and shrinks with variety: 10 training problems gave 112/112 and 111/112 E-solutions; 2 gave 0.73 and 0.55; alternating methods during training cut use to 0.16 vs 0.80.
agent_test: Vary the number of in-context worked examples (2 vs 10) and mix two methods in the examples; compare shortcut rate.

claim: Time pressure raises rigidity and a more deliberate set (Binz DBB) lowers it: speedy group 0.97/0.99 vs plain 0.82/0.55; DBB 0.57/0.37 vs plain 0.83/0.65. Binz model needs three ingredients (learning, attention, resource limit).
agent_test: Compare a low-token arm to a high-token arm on the same fixation items; check whether fixation rate rises when reasoning is cut.

claim: In chess, a familiar smothered-mate solution blocks the shorter 3-move mate; the block falls with rating: GM 100%, IM 50%, Master 18%, Candidate Master 0% found the short mate (Exp 1).
agent_test: On problems with a familiar but longer solution, count how often the model finds the shorter one; control = same problem with the familiar line removed.

claim: Experts are partly blocked: 100 rating points down cuts odds of finding the best move by 3.67 (Exp 1) and 1.82 (Exp 2); the effect vanishes on easy problems, so it depends on problem difficulty.
agent_test: Sweep item difficulty; expect a larger fixation cost where the alternative is hard to see.

claim: Experts underestimate the effect: predicted success IM 86, Master 74, CM 59 (Exp 1) vs actual 50, 18, 0; Exp 2 97/89/73 vs 92/69/35.
agent_test: Self-report of 'I checked alternatives' should not be trusted; use an external check. Compare self-rated flexibility vs measured.

claim: The block is an attention effect, not a search-length effect: gaze stays on the familiar solution squares while people say they are still looking; search time is not longer in blocked players; Sheridan and Reingold show the same decline-of-looking pattern only in those who find the optimal move.
agent_test: Log which candidates the agent actually expands (not what it says). Test whether forced re-listing of alternatives changes expansion.

claim: Gaze marks discovery in a water-jar variant: finders look less at the trained procedure two trials before discovery (F(1,34)=6.22) and much less at discovery (F=87.16, eta2 .72); 31 of 46 (67%) found the alternative before the last critical trial.
agent_test: Early-warning idea: a fall in reuse of the trained pattern precedes switching. Probe whether a drop in overlap with the earlier solution predicts a switch.

claim: The effect is not special to chess or experts: it appears in anagrams (word vs nonword attention costs), insight puzzles (high-knowledge people solve misleading baseball items .15 vs neutral .50), and in children (DeCaro).
agent_test: Use mixed-domain fixation items for the guardrail test, not chess only.

claim: Domain knowledge can create fixation, and a warning did not remove it: high-knowledge misleading .30 with warning vs .20 without, ns (N=20, 5 per cell).
agent_test: Test whether a generic prompt 'a familiar answer may be wrong' shrinks the effect. Wiley predicts no.

claim: Which de-fixation steps work is contested: warning failed (Wiley); retrieving red herrings twice made later solving worse in a reinstated context (.456 vs .539); mindfulness training lowered rigidity (1.17 vs 2.93; 2.19 vs 3.42) but did not correlate with water-jar rigidity (r=.10). LLM data add a split: on ReasoningTrap a generic hint raised Qwen3-32B accuracy on edited items from 33.25 to 45.30 (AIME) and 34.60 to 46.88 (MATH500) without hurting originals, while other hint wordings gave less (38.24, 42.11, 37.75); presenting a draft as someone else's, or appending Wait, closed 89.3% of the self-correction blind spot in 14 open models.
agent_test: Compare four arms at equal tokens: no cue, generic warning, forced alternative generation, explicit reset of the earlier method.

claim: Shortcut-first induction lowers deep understanding: shortcut use 56% vs 19% (adults), 30% vs 10% (children); conceptual knowledge differed (F=4.67; F=5.13).
agent_test: Check whether the order of examples shown first changes which method the model chooses later.

claim: Fixation can be reduced by removing the old item from memory: remembered fixation items cut target solving to 27.3% vs control 43.5%; items told to forget gave 36.7% vs 37.6%.
agent_test: Test an operation that drops or tags a failed or blocking candidate out of context versus keeping it visible.

claim: Accessibility of the right answer reduces the induction cost: low accessibility shows a cost (1.27 vs 0.70); high accessibility none (1.90 vs 2.07). Relational encoding raised insight solving from 22% to 43% (one of two problems significant).
agent_test: Re-encode the problem relationally (restate in abstract terms) before solving; compare to plain restatement.

claim: Persistence of a short-term set depends on design: after enhanced practice the unfamiliar solution is solved less often (Exp 1, N=32) but only slower, with no accuracy cost, in Exp 2 (N=28).
agent_test: Measure both accuracy and token cost; fixation may show as extra tokens, not wrong answers.

claim: Outcome feedback matters: when a pattern pays off (75% or 88% win rate), re-using the old pattern beat learning a new one (.694 vs .592; .725 vs .622); under punishment the old-pattern advantage disappeared.
agent_test: Add a negative-check signal when the first method fails and see if switching rises.

claim: LLMs show Einstellung-like fixation on red herrings: on Only Connect walls GPT-4 10-shot solved 3 of 494 walls (0-shot 6), 55 with randomised groups and 378 on the no-decoy WordNet set; more shots did not help (WordNet: 471 at 0-shot, 378 at 10-shot). CORRECTED from earlier lines.
agent_test: Run the same wall variants on the agent; check whether decoys cost more than for a plain model at equal tokens.

claim: In medical LLMs a familiar disease pattern traps models: MedEinst (5,383 pairs, 17 LLMs) bias trap rates range about 33 to 66% (Gemini-2.5-pro 60.90%, GPT-5 51.87%); higher baseline accuracy did not mean fewer traps; no size trend. Clean table read (arXiv HTML): trap rates run 33.75 (ECR-Agent) to 66.10 (Baichuan-M2-32B); Gemini-2.5-pro 60.90, GPT-5 51.87, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98, DeepSeek-R1 46.12, QwQ-32B 44.88, Qwen3-32B 43.46.
agent_test: Use a counterfactual-pair design (same evidence, one swapped feature) to measure trap rate of our schema vs plain.

claim: Multi-agent consensus did not fix the trap in MedEinst: on a clean table read, MDAgent (Qwen3-32B) had baseline accuracy 29.70, robust accuracy 10.34, trap rate 40.34 and DyLAN 32.11/8.11/41.69, against base Qwen3-32B 40.25/11.86/43.46. Both agents lost 8-10 points of accuracy and gained only 2-3 points on trap rate. A structured evidence-audit agent (ECR-Agent) reached 69.49/24.21/33.75. Debate-or-vote (Qwen2.5-7B, average 0.7205 single, 0.7691 vote, 0.6551 centralized debate) and Precise-but-Uncoupled (reviewer precision 0.861 but 33.6% uptake vs 0.644 and 93.5% for broadcast) show the same pattern outside medicine: agreeing agents add little and a correct critic must be coupled to the solver. That voting RAISES the trap rate is not shown.
agent_test: Compare single agent, agent-with-critic and multi-vote at equal tokens on counterfactual pairs.

claim: Failure modes of LLM fixation: key evidence ignored (blindness, GPT-5 in over 35% of errors); when noticed, 43% underthinking and 22% overthinking.
agent_test: Tag each wrong answer by failure mode (not seen / seen but not weighed / rationalised) in our traces.

claim: Reasoning models have improved on clinical fixation: Kim 2025 physicians 66% vs best model 52% (DeepSeek-R1); Shidara 2026 Claude 4.1 Opus 75.1% vs physicians 66%, and on the human-miss set 55% decisively correct and 25% decisively wrong.
agent_test: Re-run the 100 mARC items with our scaffold vs plain at equal tokens; report the human-miss set.

claim: LLMs are overconfident when wrong on fixation items (Kim 2025); calibration is better in newer reasoning models (Shidara 2026).
agent_test: Compare stated confidence vs correctness on fixation items; test a confidence-triggered re-check.

claim: Mental-set effect in LLMs on arithmetic: GPT-4o exact match 0.33 to 0.83 across conditions with only 6 items per cell; CoT lifts Llama to 0.5-0.83 but steps stay at 3 where humans use 1. Too small for firm conclusions.
agent_test: Replicate with at least 50 items per cell and several seeds before drawing conclusions.

claim: Self-correction without an external signal does not remove errors and may harm: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8 over two rounds; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; with oracle labels it helps (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3). Indirect evidence, not an Einstellung test. Added: with near-perfect external feedback, solvers still plateau below the target (Feedback Friction; counterfactual arithmetic never above 20% after 10 rounds), and high-confidence answers resist most.
agent_test: A fixation check should rely on an external test (run, verify), not 'think again'. Compare self-reflection vs external-check arms at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-turn drift: average 39% drop from single-turn to multi-turn; unreliability up 112%. Not Einstellung proper, but relevant to early-answer lock-in.
agent_test: Test whether early commitments in a long trace anchor later steps.

claim: Prompt-level defixation helps creative output in LLMs: IDEAFix reports gains of roughly +10% to +41% per metric across five models; numbers partly garbled in the source.
agent_test: Treat as weak. Re-test a defixation prompt on a fixation set with a measured shortcut rate.

claim: Programmers show a mental set too: 57 of 129 respondents showed at least one set; less Python experience went with more sets (p=.006); listed interventions were rated unhelpful.
agent_test: Not testable on an agent directly; supports adding fixation prompts for code tasks.

claim: Shortcut fixation also appears in neural nets: in continual learning a shortcut patch acted as a distractor for most methods; only generative replay (DGR) showed a clear penalty.
agent_test: Check whether a stale pattern in memory (a retrieved note) acts as a shortcut for the agent; compare retrieval on vs off.

claim: Chess-trained language models are brittle out of distribution, small specialised nets can beat much larger ones, and an external verifier raised move validity from 19.3 to 95.3%.
agent_test: Tie to the agent: an external legality or correctness check beats self-assessment.

claim: No paper tests the core Luchins design on a plain LLM (long method learned from in-context examples, then a shortcut missed, against a no-example control). The nearest measured designs go the other direction or use pretraining instead of in-context habit: SenseMath shows models use shortcuts on only 20-39% of strong-shortcut items under plain CoT at 4 digits, rising to 37-59% at 16 digits; ReasoningTrap shows edited items lower p-pass@1 from 75.42 to 33.25 (Qwen3-32B think, AIME).
agent_test: Run the real design: 3-5 solved long-method examples in context vs zero examples, then critical items with a shorter route; at least 30 items per cell; report shortcut rate per cell at equal tokens.

claim: Familiar-framing fixation shows in LLM reasoning traces: models say the problem resembles a famous puzzle and then apply the heavy method to a trivial question. Claude Opus 4 falls from near 100% to 85-90% as reasoning lengthens; DeepSeek R1 falls from 70% to 30% with 5 distractors; o3 recovers when distractors hide the famous framing.
agent_test: Add a rule: when the trace says 'this is like known problem X', write one line on why X's method is or is not needed before using it.

claim: Reasoning length is not a reliable cure for fixation. Across model pairs on ReasoningTrap, thinking versions did worse than non-thinking twins (Qwen3-32B 33.25 vs 45.14 AIME; 34.60 vs 50.51 MATH500; QwQ-32B 49.21 vs Qwen2.5-32B 59.12). Inside one model, higher o4-mini effort helped (MATH500 39.06 to 53.47). Extra reasoning can also turn a correct early answer wrong (first-correct-prefix stopping beats standard reasoning by up to 21%) and cut-to-low budget helps edited items (53.66) but wrecks originals (75.42 to 31.09).
agent_test: Test three arms at equal tokens: short, long, long with a checkpoint that compares the trace with the problem constraints. Do not assume a token cap or a token boost alone helps.

claim: A generic warning helps an LLM on fixation items, unlike the human Wiley result, but wording matters. Qwen3-32B on ConditionedMath: no hint 33.25 (AIME) / 34.60 (MATH500); 'unusual condition, do not overinterpret' 45.30 / 46.88; 'not a typo' 38.24 / 42.11; 'strictly follow' 41.23 / 37.75. Original items stayed level or rose.
agent_test: Include a short specific warning in the schema, but test its wording; compare against forced alternative generation and an external check at equal tokens.

claim: A measurable early signal of LLM fixation exists in the text. Counting reasoning paragraphs closer to the familiar solution than to the edited problem gives a contamination ratio; accuracy holds up to about 40% and drops sharply beyond; wrong runs contaminate more as the trace grows. The first step also matters: a wrong first step cuts final accuracy by 40% on average (r=0.60), and hidden-state similarity at step 4 tracks later stability (r=-0.35, AUROC 0.81) but not correctness.
agent_test: Log similarity of each reasoning block to the retrieved or earlier solution; trigger a restatement or a fresh opening when the share passes about 40% or when the first step matches the earlier solution.

claim: A wrong retrieved or stored memory is followed and persists. In WebArena agents a plausible but task-wrong memory is adopted at the first exposed step 63-72% of the time across five models; success after adoption is 17-31%; paired damage rises with baseline strength (2.1 pp to 25.5 pp); re-alignment after divergence is 7-15% vs 27-42% with helpful memory. Stored abstractions did worse than raw trajectories in 7 of 9 settings (49.0% vs 53.5%); on-demand guidance that is discarded did best (59.9%). Dose-response by similarity or success count is not measured.
agent_test: Treat any retrieved past solution as a hypothesis checked at step one and re-checked later; store raw cases, rebuild guidance per task. Measure harm against example similarity and number of past successes.

claim: A critic helps only if its output reaches the solver. Reviewer precision 0.861 vs 0.644 but critique changed the next answer 33.6% vs 93.5% of the time and repair rates were 0.051 vs 0.286. Models correct an error shown as someone else's but not as their own (blind spot 64.5% in 14 open models); appending Wait cut that by 89.3%. Near-perfect feedback still left solvers below target on nine tasks.
agent_test: Present the earlier answer as a third party's draft to a checker role and force a new attempt that rejects it; measure uptake as well as detection.

claim: LLM models cannot judge by themselves when a shortcut or familiar method applies: given a shortcut-applicability question, GPT-4o-mini was right on 100% of strong items and 0% of controls because it said yes to every item; Qwen3-8B 98% and 0%. Stated confidence on fixation items versus controls has still not been measured.
agent_test: Do not use a self-rated 'is the shortcut applicable' check as a gate. Measure confidence on trap vs control twins directly.

claim: A strong neural chess engine can compute the right tactic and still play a different move: in Leela Chess Zero, 8,648 forgotten positions had the correct move in middle layers and a quiet move at the end in 68.3% of cases; steering recovered 71.7% of held-out forgotten puzzles. This is a learned-prior override, not a tested familiar-longer-mate vs shorter-mate contrast.
agent_test: Compare the final answer with intermediate working; do not read it as evidence that chess engines show Bilalic's effect.

claim: MedEinst difficulty and size patterns, clean read: reasoning-tuned models do not lower the trap rate (DeepSeek-R1 46.12, QwQ-32B 44.88 vs Qwen3-32B 43.46), one of the two top-accuracy models has a high trap rate (Gemini-2.5-pro 60.90 at 53.58 accuracy) and a medical fine-tune (Baichuan-M2-32B 66.10), and the Bilalic difficulty dependence (effect gone on easy items) is untested in LLMs; SenseMath points the other way (shortcut use rises with problem size).
agent_test: Vary item difficulty within matched trap/control twins and report the trap gap per difficulty tier.
